ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: Using a frog with the brain removed but the spinal cord retained (called a spinal frog) as the material, conduct a reflex activity experiment. Please answer: Cut the efferent nerve that innervates the left hind limb of the spinal frog (see figure). If stimulation of a certain segment at the cut site produces extension and contraction activity, can this activity be called reflex activity?

ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: Using a frog with the brain removed but the spinal cord retained (called a spinal frog) as the material, conduct a reflex activity experiment. Please answer: Cut the efferent nerve that innervates the left hind limb of the spinal frog (see figure). If stimulation of a certain segment at the cut site produces extension and contraction activity, can this activity be called reflex activity?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, “nerve center” is labeled; the “afferent nerve” above points toward the nerve center; below is labeled “efferent nerve,” and the “cut site” is marked on the efferent nerve, with the two sides of the cut site labeled as end A and end B respectively. Then reason: The question says that what is cut is the efferent nerve that innervates the left hind limb of the spinal frog. Although hind limb extension and contraction activity appears after stimulating a certain segment at the cut site, a reflex must depend on a complete reflex arc, including receptor, afferent nerve, nerve center, efferent nerve, and effector. After the efferent nerve is cut, the reflex arc is already incomplete; directly stimulating a certain segment of the efferent nerve to cause muscle extension and contraction is only a response after the nerve or effector is stimulated, and is not reflex activity completed through a complete reflex arc. Therefore this activity cannot be called reflex activity.
